newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wants to expand health care to 5 mln kids.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wants to expand health care to 5 mln kids.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday asked Congress to expand health care to about half of the 10 million U.S. children now without insurance and provide short-term coverage to millions of people between jobs.
Clinton's five-year plan to balance the budget also includes an annual cap on the Medicaid health programme for the poor, elderly and disabled. But the cap is opposed by the nation's governors.

As previously announced, his budget blueprint would cut the Medicare insurance programme for the elderly by $100 billion over five years, mainly by reducing payments to doctors, hospitals and other health providers.
Expanding health insurance to children and unemployed workers is one of the main new policy initiatives in Clinton's budget, with a price of about $18.4 billion over five years.
Outlining the plan in his State of the Union address on Tuesday, Clinton declared, "We must continue step by step to give more families access to affordable, quality health care."

The president's five-year plan includes $9.8 billion in new spending to help states finance up to six months of health coverage to individuals and their families who are between jobs -- and often without insurance.
The White House estimates that such programmes would reach up to 3.2 million families, including 700,000 children.
Clinton would reach low-income children who do not have insurance by expanding coverage under Medicaid.

The White House would let states keep children on the Medicaid rolls for up to a year, rather than having to recertify their eligibility at least every six months. The budget estimates that a million children who would otherwise lose Medicaid coverage would keep it with that change.
Further, about three million poor children who now qualify for Medicaid are not enrolled. Clinton wants states to develop outreach programmes to cover such children.
The president is also calling for $750 million a year in aid to states to work with insurers, health providers, business and schools to expand coverage to a million children.

The proposal does not go as far as congressional Democrats had hoped. Senate Democrats have proposed using either refundable tax credits or vouchers to ensure health coverage to all children up to the age of 18.
As part of his balanced budget, Clinton's plan sets annual caps on Medicaid, currently an open-ended entitlement jointly funded by the states and the federal government.
The caps, based on spending per beneficiary, per year, would be combined with cuts in payments to hospitals that serve a large number of the poor to save $22 billion.
About $13 billion of those savings would be ploughed back into other Medicaid initiatives, making net savings lower.
Medicaid, which serves about 37 million Americans, has long been one of the fastest growing programmes in state budgets, comprising about 20 percent of spending on average.

Liberal Democrats oppose the caps, saying if growth is higher than expected, states will have to cut services to the poor. The National Governors' Association also opposes a cap on the grounds it would shift costs to states.

The Medicare budget provisions were announced by Democrat Clinton weeks ago in a bid to compromise with majority Republicans in Congress. The future of Medicare was a major battleground of last November's election, with Democrats claimng Republican-proposed "cuts" would destroy the programme.

Saying he was trying to meet Republicans halfway on the politically sensitive issue, Clinton has proposed $100 billion in cuts over five years, $138 billion over six. Those cuts, mainly in payments to hospitals, doctors and managed care plans, are deeper than Clinton was previously willing to go.

The White House says its plan would ensure the solvency for the next 10 years of Medicare's Part A hospital trust fund, facing pending bankruptcy. Republicans say Clinton's plan bases the solvency claim on phony accounting gimmicks.

The plan freezes Part B doctors' premiums at 25 percent rather than letting them fall further as allowed under current law, but it does not include a controversial proposal to make well-off recipients pay higher premiums.
